case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s bar on relitigating claims in “second or successive” habeas applications—28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1)—applies to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive motions to vacate sentence under 28 U.S.C. §2255, and whether the Supreme Court can review courts of appeals’ authorization decisions despite §2244(b)(3)(E).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 2244(b)(1), 2244(b)(3)(E), and 2255 (especially the second-or-successive gatekeeping framework and §2255(f)(3) limitations rule as discussed); AEDPA generally.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that §2244(b)(1) by its text applies only to state-prisoner habeas petitions under §2254 (“application” in §2244(b) is tied to §2254), and Congress created a separate, self-contained second-or-successive regime for federal prisoners in §2255(h) that does not incorporate §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim-repetition bar; he further contends that reading §2244(b)(1) into §2255 improperly adds hurdles beyond what Congress imposed, exacerbates unfairness when the law changes after a prisoner’s first collateral attack, and entrenches a circuit split that otherwise evades review because §2244(b)(3)(E) is invoked to block certiorari review of authorization denials.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States maintains that AEDPA’s gatekeeping provisions for second-or-successive filings operate as an integrated scheme in which §2244(b)(1)’s claim-preclusion rule applies equally to federal-prisoner §2255 motions, and that this reading promotes AEDPA’s central goal of finality by preventing repetitive litigation after prisoners have already had multiple chances (trial/direct appeal/first §2255); the government also relies on §2244(b)(3)(E) to argue that the Supreme Court lacks certiorari jurisdiction to review court-of-appeals authorization decisions granting or denying leave to file a second-or-successive §2255 motion (or at least that review is tightly limited), meaning the authorization ruling itself is insulated from certiorari review.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (statement respecting denial of certiorari by Justice Kavanaugh)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (statement respecting denial by Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Jackson)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch raise the strongest objection: §2244(b)(1) is expressly limited to “application[s] under section 2254,” and we should be wary of extending that language to §2255 by implication. But §2255(h)’s directive that a successive motion may proceed only if “certified as provided in section 2244,” read in AEDPA’s integrated gatekeeping design, most naturally incorporates the operative second-or-successive constraints in §2244(b) that make certification determinate, not merely the mechanics of §2244(b)(3). On reviewability, I agree with Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh that the proposed “antecedent legal question” carve-out is hard to reconcile with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar and Felker’s acceptance of Congress’s channeling; a minimalist approach counsels against creating an atextual exception that would invite relabeling. I would keep our holding narrow—tied to the specific cross-reference in §2255(h) and Felker—without opining on broader constitutional questions or any distinct original-habeas avenue.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Kagan’s best point is textual: §2244(b)(1) expressly targets “application[s] under section 2254,” and we should not erase that limitation by implication. But §2255(h) does not merely borrow a filing formality; it conditions a second or successive §2255 motion on certification “as provided in section 2244,” and in AEDPA’s structure that naturally incorporates the operative gatekeeping limits that define what may be authorized, not just the mechanics of §2244(b)(3). On reviewability, I do not see how an “antecedent legal question” carve-out can be reconciled with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar on certiorari to “review” authorization decisions; as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh note, Felker counsels taking Congress’s channeling as written rather than inviting relabeling that would swallow the jurisdictional rule. Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concerns are serious, but under Dodd we enforce AEDPA’s enacted constraints even when harsh, and the petitioners have not identified text clearly preserving our certiorari jurisdiction or excluding §2244(b)(1) from the incorporated scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is the express limitation in §2244(b)(1) to “application[s] under section 2254,” and I agree we cannot simply erase those words. But §2255(h)’s direction that a second motion may proceed only if “certified as provided in section 2244,” read as an operative incorporation in AEDPA’s gatekeeping scheme (as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize), is most naturally understood to bring along the substantive second-or-successive constraints that make certification meaningful—including the no-repetition rule—rather than importing only (b)(3)’s mechanics and leaving a conspicuous federal-state asymmetry that undermines AEDPA’s finality aims. On reviewability, Justice Gorsuch’s proposed “antecedent legal question” carveout cannot be squared with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s unqualified prohibition on certiorari “to review” authorization decisions; Felker supports respecting that channeling choice, and recognizing an exception would invite routine relabeling that effectively nullifies the bar. Dodd reinforces that we apply AEDPA’s harsh limits as written in the successive-review context, and I do not see a textual basis to treat §2255(h)’s cross-reference as selectively importing only the parts petitioners prefer.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s “integrated scheme” reading is the strongest case for Respondent, but it cannot overcome the express textual limitation in §2244(b)(1) to “application[s] under section 2254”; Congress knew how to write a relitigation bar for §2255 and did not. Even accepting that §2255(h) must incorporate more than “paperwork,” the most natural import from “as provided in section 2244” is the (b)(3) certification mechanism and its standards, not a §2254-only claim-preclusion rule—especially where liberty interests and later-revealed legal error are at stake. On reviewability, Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E) and Felker is serious, but Felker does not require reading the certiorari bar to insulate an antecedent statutory-scope question from any correction, and I would construe that jurisdictional bar narrowly rather than invite circuit entrenchment of AEDPA’s meaning. Dodd’s admonition to apply harsh statutes as written cuts against Respondent here because the harshness they seek is not written into §2255(h).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s “integrated scheme” point is the strongest structural case for Respondent, but it cannot overcome the specific textual limitation in §2244(b)(1) to an “application under section 2254”; under a pragmatic textualism, §2255(h)’s phrase “certified as provided in section 2244” most naturally incorporates the certification mechanism in §2244(b)(3), not a §2254-only substantive relitigation bar. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s asymmetry concern is a plausible policy intuition, yet AEDPA repeatedly draws and maintains §2254/§2255 distinctions, so I do not think we should “complete” the scheme by importing language Congress chose to confine to §2254. On reviewability, Justice Thomas’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E) and Felker is serious, but Felker’s acceptance of channeling does not require reading (b)(3)(E) to bar our review of the antecedent statutory-scope question; otherwise courts of appeals could entrench divergent interpretations of AEDPA’s cross-references with no possibility of correction. Dodd’s admonition to enforce harsh text, invoked by Justice Alito, cuts against Respondent here because the harsh extra bar they seek is not enacted in §2255(h) and (b)(1) is textually cabined to §2254.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas offer the strongest Respondent argument: §2255(h)’s instruction that certification occur “as provided in section 2244” should be read as importing §2244(b)’s operative second-or-successive limits, including (b)(1). But as a textualist, I cannot treat that cross-reference as silently rewriting §2244(b)(1)’s express limitation to an “application under section 2254”; Congress knew how to write §2255-specific relitigation language and did not. On jurisdiction, Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E) and Felker is serious, yet Felker’s channeling holding does not compel reading (b)(3)(E) to bar our review of the antecedent statutory-scope question whether (b)(1) applies to §2255 at all—otherwise courts of appeals would have the final word on AEDPA’s meaning with no possibility of correction. Dodd’s insistence on applying AEDPA as written cuts against Respondent because the “written” text draws the §2254/§2255 line, and structural finality instincts cannot justify erasing it.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan make the best textual point that §2244(b)(1) expressly refers to an “application under section 2254,” but §2255(h)’s command that a second motion be “certified as provided in section 2244” is, in AEDPA’s gatekeeping architecture emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett, most naturally read to incorporate the operative second-or-successive limits that define what may be authorized, not just the (b)(3) filing mechanics. I also remain persuaded by Justice Thomas that §2244(b)(3)(E)’s bar on certiorari to “review” an authorization decision is categorical, and Felker accepts Congress’s channeling; the proposed “antecedent legal question” carve-out would invite routine relabeling and effectively nullify (E) in a way that is hard to square with the text and with institutional respect for jurisdictional limits. Justice Sotomayor’s fairness concerns are serious, but under Dodd and our usual institutionalist approach, those considerations cannot justify selectively importing only the convenient parts of §2244 while disregarding the parts that make the cross-reference function coherently. No colleague has identified a precedent that materially undercuts Felker’s treatment of Congress’s restriction or supplies a principled textual basis for the suggested reviewability exception.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan press the best textual objection: §2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to an “application under section 2254,” and §2255(h) does not repeat that phrase. But the cross-reference in §2255(h)—certification “as provided in section 2244”—is most naturally read, in AEDPA’s integrated gatekeeping architecture emphasized by the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas, to incorporate the operative constraints that define what may be authorized (including the relitigation bar), not merely the mechanics of §2244(b)(3); otherwise the court of appeals’ authorization role becomes untethered from §2244(b)’s substantive limits in a way Congress is unlikely to have intended. On reviewability, Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s proposed “antecedent legal question” carve-out cannot be squared with §2244(b)(3)(E)’s categorical bar on certiorari to “review a decision of a court of appeals,” and Felker supports honoring that channeling rather than creating an atextual exception that invites relabeling. Dodd reinforces that we apply AEDPA’s limitations as written even when they operate harshly, which counsels against narrowing (b)(3)(E) or treating the §2255(h) cross-reference as selectively importing only procedures.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s “integrated scheme” account is the Respondent’s strongest point, but it still asks us to treat §2255(h)’s phrase “as provided in section 2244” as silently importing a substantive relitigation bar that Congress textually confined to “application[s] under section 2254” in §2244(b)(1). Under my pragmatic, fairness-oriented methodology, structural coherence cannot override an enacted statutory line—especially where §2255(h) already contains strict substantive triggers and where adding §2244(b)(1) would predictably foreclose review of serious error without clear textual authorization. On jurisdiction, I take Justice Kavanaugh’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on §2244(b)(3)(E) and Felker seriously, but Felker’s acceptance of channeling does not compel reading (b)(3)(E) to insulate an antecedent, purely legal question about whether §2244(b)(1) applies to §2255 at all; that broader reading would create unreviewable circuit entrenchment with major uniformity and legitimacy costs. Dodd’s admonition to apply AEDPA as written cuts against Respondent here because the writing Congress chose limits §2244(b)(1) to §2254 and does not replicate that limit in §2255(h).

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA establishes an integrated second-or-successive gatekeeping scheme, and §2255(h) expressly incorporates §2244’s procedures, making it most consistent with the statute’s structure and finality aims to apply §2244(b)(1)’s claim-repetition bar to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive §2255 motions as well. On Supreme Court review, §2244(b)(3)(E) by its terms removes certiorari jurisdiction over courts of appeals’ gatekeeping authorizations, and Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996), upheld that limitation while noting alternative avenues (including original habeas) and leaving broader Exceptions Clause questions for another day. In a minimalist posture, I would follow Felker’s reading and avoid any constitutional confrontation by accepting the jurisdictional bar here and resolving the case on statutory grounds. This approach also promotes institutional legitimacy by respecting Congress’s calibrated limits in AEDPA and avoiding a broad rewrite of the second-or-successive framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Reading AEDPA as a coherent textual scheme, §2255(h) expressly requires a federal prisoner to obtain certification “as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b) is the provision that defines the consequences of a second-or-successive filing—including §2244(b)(1)’s categorical bar on re-presenting claims previously raised. Nothing in §2255(h)’s text affirmatively excludes §2244(b)(1), and importing a claim-repetition bar accords with AEDPA’s evident design to limit serial collateral attacks and promote finality. As to reviewability, §2244(b)(3)(E) states that an authorization decision by the court of appeals “shall not be the subject of a petition for rehearing or for a writ of certiorari,” and under Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996), Congress may restrict certiorari review of gatekeeping determinations so long as some avenue (e.g., original habeas) remains, avoiding an Exceptions Clause problem. The statute’s plain text therefore bars certiorari review of the authorization decision itself, even if other routes for Supreme Court review may exist in a proper case.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: AEDPA’s successive-filing provisions operate as an integrated gatekeeping scheme aimed at finality, and reading §2244(b)(1)’s categorical bar on relitigating previously presented claims to apply to second-or-successive §2255 motions best effectuates that structure and purpose, rather than creating an atextual carve-out for federal prisoners. Section 2244(b)(3)(E) states in unqualified terms that the court of appeals’ authorization decision “shall not be appealable and shall not be the subject of a petition for a writ of certiorari,” and under Felker v. Turpin we should respect Congress’s channeling of review while recognizing that any residual “original habeas” authority does not justify routine certiorari review of gatekeeping orders. This reading avoids practical consequences that would invite repetitive litigation after trial, direct appeal, and an initial §2255 motion, undermining AEDPA’s central goals. Consistent with Dodd v. United States, we should adhere to the statutory text and Congress’s calibrated limits on postconviction review even when they operate harshly in particular cases.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs “second or successive” habeas “applications” in the §2254/state-prisoner framework, while Congress separately crafted §2255(h) to regulate federal prisoners’ second-or-successive motions without importing §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim-repetition bar; reading that extra bar into §2255 risks foreclosing merits review even when later legal developments reveal serious sentencing or conviction error, a result in tension with fairness and access to justice. On Supreme Court review, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s jurisdiction-stripping should be construed narrowly to avoid insulating an entrenched circuit split from any meaningful correction, particularly where the authorization regime effectively determines whether a potentially meritorious constitutional claim can ever be heard. Felker v. Turpin teaches that Congress’s limits on this Court’s review of successive-petition gatekeeping must be read with constitutional avoidance in mind, and that some avenues of Supreme Court oversight remain necessary to preserve this Court’s essential role. Given AEDPA’s severe practical consequences for prisoners with no other route to vindicate rights, I would not extend §2244(b)(1) beyond its text and would allow review to resolve the conflict.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Textually, §2244(b)(1) speaks to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and Congress separately set out the federal-prisoner gatekeeping rule in §2255(h) without importing §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim-repetition bar; reading (b)(1) into §2255 adds a hurdle Congress did not enact and disrupts AEDPA’s internal coherence. On reviewability, §2244(b)(3)(E) bars certiorari to “review a decision of a court of appeals” on the authorization request, but under Felker v. Turpin the Court should not treat that language as insulating antecedent, purely legal questions about the scope of the gatekeeping regime itself—especially where the court of appeals’ denial rests on an inapplicable provision rather than a (b)(3)(C)-type authorization determination. This narrower construction preserves workability and uniformity by allowing this Court to resolve the threshold statutory-interpretation issue driving an entrenched circuit split. AEDPA’s finality interests remain protected because §2255(h)’s strict criteria and the one-year limit in §2255(f)(3) still constrain successive federal collateral attacks.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The text of §2244(b)(1) speaks to "a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254," so its categorical claim-repetition bar does not, by its plain terms, govern federal prisoners’ second-or-successive motions under §2255, which Congress separately regulated in §2255(h). Reading §2244(b)(1) into §2255 would add an extra-jurisdictional hurdle Congress did not enact and would upset the carefully drawn scheme AEDPA created for federal collateral review (cf. Dodd v. United States, 545 U.S. 353 (2005) (enforcing AEDPA’s text as written)). As for review, §2244(b)(3)(E) bars certiorari over a court of appeals’ discretionary authorization decision, but under Felker v. Turpin, 518 U.S. 651 (1996), that bar should not be extended to insulate from this Court’s review the antecedent, purely legal question whether §2244(b)(1) applies to §2255 at all; otherwise courts of appeals could conclusively decide questions of statutory scope without Supreme Court correction, raising serious structural concerns. Consistent with separation-of-powers principles and ordinary appellate review of legal boundaries, I would hold §2244(b)(1) inapplicable to §2255 and allow review at least of the courts of appeals’ threshold legal determination about AEDPA’s reach.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA’s second-or-successive framework is best read as an integrated scheme: §2255(h) expressly requires appellate “certification” and that certification process is supplied by §2244(b)(3), making it natural—and more workable—to apply §2244(b)(1)’s claim-repetition bar to successive §2255 motions to promote finality and prevent repetitive litigation. The statutory structure and AEDPA’s settled purpose counsel against creating a broader successive-collateral-review opportunity for federal prisoners than for state prisoners absent a clear textual command, especially given the practical burdens on courts and the system’s reliance on finality after trial, appeal, and the first §2255 motion. On Supreme Court review, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s jurisdictional bar is controlling; under Felker v. Turpin, the Court has upheld that restriction and has cautioned against reading around AEDPA’s express limits on certiorari review, preserving legitimacy by adhering to the statute’s clear channeling of review. Consistent with that precedent and judicial restraint, I would not expand certiorari jurisdiction over courts of appeals’ authorization decisions in the face of §2244(b)(3)(E).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually, AEDPA’s second-or-successive provisions function as an integrated gatekeeping scheme: §2255(h) directs federal prisoners into the same authorization mechanism set out in §2244(b)(3), and the closely linked claim-repetition bar in §2244(b)(1) is best read to apply to that same category of “second or successive” collateral attacks to prevent relitigation and promote finality. That reading fits AEDPA’s structure and purpose, and avoids creating an atextual asymmetry in which state prisoners face a categorical bar on repeated claims while federal prisoners do not, despite parallel gatekeeping triggers. As to review, §2244(b)(3)(E) expressly provides that the courts of appeals’ authorization decisions “shall not be the subject of … a petition for a writ of certiorari,” and Felker v. Turpin counsels that we read such jurisdiction-stripping provisions as written while recognizing (and not reaching here) the separate possibility of original-habeas review. Precedent emphasizing strict adherence to AEDPA’s text in the collateral-review context, including Dodd v. United States, reinforces that courts should not soften statutory limits based on equitable concerns about later changes in law.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms governs “applications” for habeas relief in the §2254 state-prisoner framework, while Congress separately enacted a self-contained gatekeeping regime for federal prisoners in §2255(h); importing §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim-repetition bar into §2255 adds a hurdle Congress did not clearly impose and risks unfairness when intervening law emerges after a first collateral attack. On Supreme Court review, §2244(b)(3)(E) should be read narrowly as Felker v. Turpin instructs, and absent an unmistakable clear statement this Court should not treat it as broadly divesting jurisdiction to resolve important statutory conflicts that otherwise evade review. That narrow reading is consistent with the caution reflected in Castro v. United States against expansive jurisdiction-stripping constructions and helps ensure procedurally fair, uniform application of AEDPA across circuits. Practical consequences also favor allowing review where the authorization decision turns on a pure question of statutory interpretation affecting access to collateral review.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether AEDPA’s claim-bar in 28 U.S.C. §2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners’ second-or-successive motions under 28 U.S.C. §2255 (and, relatedly, whether §2244(b)(3)(E) blocks Supreme Court certiorari review of court-of-appeals authorization decisions in §2255 successive-motion proceedings).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. §§ 2244(b)(1), 2244(b)(3)(E), and 2255 (including the AEDPA second-or-successive regime and, by analogy, AEDPA’s limitations framework reflected in §2255(f)(3)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Bowe argues that §2244(b)(1)—which by its text governs claims presented in a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254”—should not be imported into §2255 proceedings for federal prisoners. He contends that Congress created a distinct successive-motion gatekeeping scheme for §2255 in §2255(h), and that layering §2244(b)(1)’s categorical ‘claim presented’ bar on top of §2255(h) imposes an extra-statutory, harsher limitation not enacted for federal prisoners. He also maintains that if courts read §2244(b)(3)(E) to bar certiorari review of authorization denials/grants in §2255 cases, the Court should still take the case (or find a jurisdictional path) because otherwise a major circuit split on the scope of §2244(b)(1) in §2255 cases becomes effectively unreviewable.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States maintains that applying §2244(b)(1) to §2255 successive motions is consistent with AEDPA’s design to tighten repetitive postconviction litigation and promote finality, and that federal prisoners are not unfairly disadvantaged because AEDPA routinely withholds the benefit of later legal developments even from diligent prisoners. It points to AEDPA’s one-year limitations rule in §2255(f)(3), as interpreted in Dodd v. United States, to argue that Congress accepted ‘harsh’ results and prioritized finality over equitable access to new rules. The government also relies on the view that §2244(b)(3)(E) restricts Supreme Court review of court-of-appeals authorization decisions, which (in its view) counsels against certiorari jurisdiction over those gatekeeping determinations.
key_precedents: Avery v. United States, 140 S. Ct. 1080 (2020) (Kavanaugh, J., statement respecting denial of certiorari)
In re Bowe, 144 S. Ct. 1170 (2024) (Sotomayor, J., statement respecting denial, joined by Jackson, J.)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan raise the Petitioner’s strongest point: §2244(b)(1) by its terms applies only to an application under §2254, and we should hesitate to let a cross-reference “erase” that limiting phrase. But I agree with Justice Thomas (and Justice Kavanaugh) that §2255(h)’s command that a successive motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” combined with §2244(b)(3)(C)’s requirement that “the application” satisfy “the requirements of this subsection,” most naturally sweeps in subsection (b)(1) as part of the incorporated certification standard rather than a merits-only rule confined to state cases. On my minimalist approach, I am reluctant to adopt Petitioner’s reading because it effectively treats (b)(1) as the one “requirement” in subsection (b) that drops out of the certification inquiry without a clear textual signal, creating an unexpressed federal/state asymmetry; Dodd reinforces that we should not soften AEDPA’s cross-referenced gatekeeping architecture where Congress wrote it in rigid terms. Justice Gorsuch’s avoidance concerns are substantial, but I see them as bearing more on how we construe §2244(b)(3)(E)’s review bar than on whether (b)(1) is among the “requirements” incorporated by (b)(3)(C).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan press the best opposing point: §2244(b)(1) by its terms applies only to an application “under section 2254,” and we should not delete that limitation by indirection. But §2255(h) commands that a successive federal-prisoner motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b)(3)(C) makes certification turn on whether “the application” satisfies “the requirements of this subsection”—language that naturally reaches all of subsection (b)’s requirements, including (b)(1)’s no-repeat-claims rule, rather than only those we deem procedurally “mechanical.” Chief Justice Roberts is right that Dodd counsels enforcing AEDPA’s cross-referenced rigidity as written, not narrowing the incorporated “requirements” to avoid harsh results or to preserve a perceived §2254/§2255 symmetry. The §2254 label in (b)(1) is not “erased” so much as it is made operative at the certification stage through Congress’s chosen incorporation-by-reference, and I do not see a textual basis to carve (b)(1) out of the “requirements of this subsection.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan make the opposing side’s best point: §2244(b)(1) expressly refers to an application “under section 2254,” and we should hesitate to extend that language by indirection. But Justice Thomas’s structural reading is more faithful to the cross-referenced scheme Congress enacted—§2255(h) requires certification “as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b)(3)(C) turns certification on satisfying “the requirements of this subsection,” which most naturally includes the no-repeat-claims rule in §2244(b)(1). Reading “requirements” to mean “all of subsection (b) except the one Congress wrote most categorically” is not textualism; it is selective incorporation that creates an atextual loophole for repetitive federal-prisoner claims. Dodd’s admonition against judicially softening AEDPA’s rigid gatekeeping supports enforcing this integrated architecture as written, and Justice Gorsuch’s Felker-based avoidance concerns are better addressed, if at all, in construing §2244(b)(3)(E)’s review bar rather than by excising §2244(b)(1) from the incorporated certification requirements.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest point: §2255(h)’s "certified as provided in section 2244" plus §2244(b)(3)(C)’s "requirements of this subsection" can be read to pull in §2244(b)(1). But that reading only works by treating the cross-referenced certification mechanism as silently overriding §2244(b)(1)’s explicit limitation to "an … application under section 2254," which (as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize) we should not delete by indirection—especially where Congress separately and specifically set the substantive successive-motion gates in §2255(h). The Chief’s reliance on Dodd reinforces my view that we enforce AEDPA’s harsh limits when Congress clearly writes them; here the added harshness depends on importing a categorical bar Congress textually confined to the §2254 track. Given the access-to-justice consequences for federal prisoners, I would require a clearer statement before extending §2244(b)(1) beyond its stated scope and would treat §2244(b)(3) as the procedure, not an expansion of §2255(h)’s substantive limits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the best opposing point: §2255(h)’s certification “as provided in section 2244,” plus §2244(b)(3)(C)’s reference to “the requirements of this subsection,” could be read to sweep in §2244(b)(1). But on a pragmatic textualist reading, we must give operative effect to §2244(b)(1)’s express limitation to “an application under section 2254,” and it is hard to square that limiting phrase with treating (b)(1) as a universal gate for §2255 motions without effectively deleting words Congress chose. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Dodd underscores enforcing AEDPA’s rigidity as written, yet here the extra rigidity comes from extending a §2254-specific categorical bar into §2255 despite §2255(h)’s distinct, self-contained substantive criteria. The more coherent integration is that §2255(h) borrows §2244(b)(3)’s procedural certification mechanism, while §2255(h) supplies the applicable substantive “requirements” for federal prisoners.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s incorporation chain is the Respondent’s best point: §2255(h) demands certification “as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b)(3)(C) asks whether “the application” meets “the requirements of this subsection.” But on a textualist reading, one of those “requirements”—§2244(b)(1)—is explicitly conditional on a defined object: “a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and I cannot treat a cross-referenced certification instruction as silently rewriting that limitation without effectively deleting words Congress chose. The better reading is that §2255(h) imports §2244(b)(3)’s gatekeeping procedure (who decides, when, and under what showing) while leaving vehicle-specific substantive bars where Congress placed them, as Justice Barrett emphasizes. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Dodd cuts against judicial softening of enacted limits, but it does not authorize adding a new categorical bar to §2255 via indirection where Congress wrote none.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan have the strongest textual objection: §2244(b)(1) by its terms governs only a successive “application under section 2254,” and we should hesitate to treat a cross-reference as deleting that limiting phrase. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas that §2255(h)’s requirement that a successive motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” coupled with §2244(b)(3)(C)’s command that certification may issue only if “the application” satisfies “the requirements of this subsection,” most naturally imports subsection (b)’s gatekeeping requirements—including (b)(1)—into the authorization decision. Dodd reinforces an institutionalist reluctance to create implied carveouts from AEDPA’s cross-referenced rigidity, and I do not think Felker’s avoidance concerns justify narrowing the incorporated certification standard rather than addressing any review-bar issue under §2244(b)(3)(E). On balance, the petitioner reading makes §2255(h)’s cross-reference oddly underinclusive and generates an unexplained federal/state asymmetry that Congress did not clearly signal.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s incorporation chain—§2255(h) cross-referencing §2244, and §2244(b)(3)(C) asking whether the application meets “the requirements of this subsection”—is the Respondent’s strongest textual point. But on a textualist reading, §2244(b)(1) is itself a requirement only for “a second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” so treating it as a freestanding “requirement” for §2255 motions makes the §2254 limitation do no work and effectively rewrites the scope Congress specified. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Dodd reinforces fidelity to AEDPA’s rigidity where Congress clearly enacted it; here the question is whether Congress clearly extended a §2254-only categorical bar to §2255, and the text cuts the other way because §2255(h) separately supplies the substantive gates for federal prisoners while borrowing §2244(b)(3)’s certification procedure. The asserted federal/state asymmetry noted by Justice Kavanaugh may be awkward, but it is not a license to override vehicle-specific statutory language through an indirection that dilutes §2244(b)(1)’s express limitation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Kavanaugh press the hardest point: §2255(h) incorporates certification “as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b)(3)(C) asks whether the application satisfies “the requirements of this subsection,” which they read to include §2244(b)(1). But that structural chain cannot do the decisive work they assign it without treating §2244(b)(1)’s explicit “under section 2254” limitation as surplusage—an interpretive move I resist, particularly where Congress separately set out the substantive successive-motion limits for federal prisoners in §2255(h). Chief Justice Roberts’s invocation of Dodd reinforces that we apply AEDPA’s strict limits when Congress clearly wrote them; here, the strictness Respondent seeks depends on extending a §2254-specific categorical bar to §2255 by indirection rather than clear text. Consistent with my procedural-fairness focus and practical-consequences lens, I would require a clearer statement before adopting an interpretation that categorically forecloses potentially meritorious federal-prisoner claims through a cross-reference.

John Roberts.reasoning: AEDPA’s successive-petition regime reflects a unified design to curb repetitive collateral attacks and promote finality, and this Court has repeatedly adhered to AEDPA’s text and structure even when that produces “harsh result[s].” Dodd v. United States, 545 U.S. 353, 359–60 (2005), is particularly instructive in the §2255 context: it declined to soften AEDPA’s limits on successive federal-prisoner litigation based on equitable concerns, underscoring Congress’s choice to prioritize finality. Given that much of §2244(b)’s gatekeeping framework has long been applied by courts in §2255 successive-motion practice, reading §2244(b)(1)’s claim-bar to apply in that setting is the narrower, institutionally stabilizing course that avoids creating a federal/state asymmetry absent a clear congressional directive. And if §2244(b)(3)(E) is read to bar certiorari review of authorization decisions, that jurisdictional limitation should be respected as written, leaving any adjustment to Congress rather than judicial revision of AEDPA’s scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and cross-references enacted by Congress point to applying §2244(b)(1)’s claim-bar in the §2255 successive-motion certification process: §2255(h) requires a second-or-successive motion to be “certified as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b)(3)(C) authorizes filing only if the application satisfies “the requirements of this subsection,” which include §2244(b)(1). Although §2244(b)(1) refers to applications “under section 2254,” Congress’s choice to legislate by cross-reference makes that requirement operative through §2244(b)(3)(C)’s incorporation when courts of appeals perform §2255(h) certification. That reading is reinforced by AEDPA’s strict, finality-focused scheme and this Court’s refusal to soften clear statutory limits in analogous §2255 contexts, see Dodd v. United States, 545 U.S. 353 (2005).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Although §2244(b)(1) is phrased in terms of a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” §2255(h) adopts AEDPA’s same gatekeeping architecture for federal successive collateral attacks, and the most sensible reading is that Congress meant to import the core anti-repetitive-litigation limits that make the scheme function. Reading §2255(h) to omit §2244(b)(1)’s claim-bar would invite claim-splitting and serial relitigation by federal prisoners, undermining AEDPA’s finality and law-enforcement interests that the statute was enacted to protect. This Court has recognized in analogous contexts that AEDPA can impose rigid, even harsh, timing and procedural rules in the federal-prisoner setting, and we have applied the text as written notwithstanding equitable objections. See Dodd v. United States, 545 U.S. 353 (2005) (enforcing §2255(f)(3)’s strict limitations structure even though it can foreclose relief).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and Congress separately created the successive-motion gatekeeping regime for federal prisoners in §2255(h); importing §2244(b)(1)’s categorical “claim presented” bar into §2255 adds a harsher, extra-textual restriction on federal prisoners that Congress did not enact. AEDPA’s purpose of finality cannot justify overriding the statutory line Congress drew, especially where the practical effect is to foreclose merits review of substantial constitutional claims and to exacerbate unfairness for prisoners least able to navigate shifting law. Dodd v. United States underscores that AEDPA already produces harsh timing results under §2255(f)(3), but that is all the more reason to resist layering additional nontextual barriers on access to postconviction review. Finally, reading §2244(b)(3)(E) to preclude this Court’s certiorari review of §2255 authorization decisions would insulate a major statutory question from correction and entrench inequitable disparities across circuits, contrary to the Court’s role in ensuring uniform federal law.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and Congress separately enacted a tailored successive-motion regime for federal prisoners in §2255(h); importing §2244(b)(1)’s categorical claim-bar into §2255 adds an extra textual hurdle that Congress did not write. The better reading is that §2255(h) supplies the exclusive gatekeeping standard for federal successive motions, while §2244(b)(3)’s authorization procedure can operate without smuggling in §2244(b)(1)’s distinct §2254 limitation, preserving statutory coherence and administrability. Tyler v. Cain underscores that AEDPA’s cross-referenced successive-motion scheme must be applied as written—particularly the specific conditions Congress set for successive filings—rather than expanded beyond the text in the name of finality. On the related point, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s bar on certiorari for “an application” should not be read to make this important §2255 question effectively unreviewable, especially where the dispute concerns the scope of a restriction that textually targets §2254 applications, not §2255 motions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its plain terms governs claims presented in a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and Congress did not write parallel language for federal-prisoner motions under §2255; as a textualist, I will not extend an express §2254-only claim bar to a different remedial scheme. While §2255(h) requires certification “as provided in section 2244,” that cross-reference is best read to import the gatekeeping procedures and standards for authorization (e.g., §2244(b)(3)), not to silently transplant §2244(b)(1)’s categorical dismissal rule that Congress limited to §2254. Reading §2244(b)(1) into §2255 would also upset separation-of-powers values by allowing courts to add an extra-statutory hurdle to congressionally prescribed collateral review, and any lingering ambiguity in this penal/postconviction context should be resolved against enlarging bars to review. Finally, consistent with Felker v. Turpin, we should construe §2244(b)(3)(E) narrowly to avoid serious constitutional questions about foreclosing this Court’s review where doing so would leave an entrenched circuit split effectively uncorrectable.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: AEDPA’s text and structure indicate that §2244(b)(1)’s claim bar applies in second-or-successive §2255 proceedings because §2255(h) conditions authorization on certification “as provided in section 2244,” and §2244(b)(3)(C) requires the applicant to satisfy the “requirements of this subsection,” which includes §2244(b)(1)’s command that repeat claims “shall be dismissed.” That reading fits AEDPA’s history-and-tradition of prioritizing finality and limiting repetitive collateral attacks, and it is practically workable because it establishes a clear, administrable rule against do-over claims. Dodd v. United States confirms that AEDPA sometimes yields harsh results by design and that courts should not soften those limits beyond what Congress enacted. Finally, §2244(b)(3)(E)’s bar on “appeal or … petition for rehearing” of authorization decisions counsels against expansive Supreme Court review of gatekeeping determinations, and in any event the better course is judicial restraint and adherence to the statute’s cross-referenced framework rather than creating exceptions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and that text does not naturally extend to federal prisoners’ successive motions governed by §2255 and its separate gatekeeping provision in §2255(h). Reading §2244(b)(1)’s categorical “claim presented” bar into §2255 would add an extra limitation Congress did not enact for federal prisoners, contrary to a textualist approach and the distinct statutory structure AEDPA set up for §2254 versus §2255. The government’s appeal to AEDPA’s general purpose and to Dodd v. United States (construing §2255(f)(3)) cannot overcome the specific limiting language Congress used in §2244(b)(1). As to §2244(b)(3)(E), Felker v. Turpin confirms Congress can bar certiorari review of gatekeeping decisions, but that jurisdictional bar does not justify importing §2244(b)(1) into §2255 where the threshold question is whether §2244(b)(1) applies at all.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2244(b)(1) by its terms applies to a “second or successive habeas corpus application under section 2254,” and importing that categorical “claim presented” bar into §2255 adds a restriction Congress did not place in §2255(h), which already provides a distinct successive-motion gatekeeping scheme for federal prisoners. Whatever overlap exists through §2255(h)’s requirement that a successive motion be “certified as provided in section 2244,” that cross-reference most naturally incorporates the authorization procedure in §2244(b)(3), not §2244(b)(1)’s separate claim-preclusion rule tied textually to §2254. Dodd v. United States confirms AEDPA can yield harsh results, but it does not justify reading extra hurdles into §2255 beyond the statute’s text—especially given the fairness and systemic-consequence concerns in foreclosing review of potentially meritorious claims. For the related jurisdiction question, extending §2244(b)(3)(E)’s certiorari bar—framed in terms of an “application”—to §2255 “motions” would close off meaningful Supreme Court review of an important statutory split without a clear congressional statement, a caution reflected in Castro v. United States.
